focus: recovery, follow-up, sports, recurrence, and integration

questions.learning_objective: Assess recovery using symptoms, ventricular function, rhythm, biomarkers, and tissue/inflammation context rather than a single variable.
questions.stem: A 15-year-old is recovering from myocarditis. Which statement best describes a sound follow-up assessment?

options.text: Recovery should integrate symptoms, ventricular function, rhythm assessment, biomarkers, and imaging/tissue findings as appropriate to the phenotype
Normal ejection fraction alone proves complete recovery
Normal troponin alone proves complete recovery
Feeling well alone is sufficient for discharge from cardiology follow-up
A normal chest radiograph is the definitive recovery test

questions.rationale: Myocarditis can recover unevenly across symptoms, pump function, inflammation, scar, and electrical stability. Follow-up therefore needs a multiparametric assessment tailored to the initial severity and residual abnormalities.

option_explanations.multidomain: Correct. This approach reduces the risk of clearing a patient while another clinically important domain remains abnormal.
option_explanations.ef_only: EF can normalize despite persistent LGE, symptoms, or arrhythmia. It is necessary information but not a complete recovery definition.
option_explanations.troponin_only: Troponin may normalize before tissue or electrical recovery and is not a stand-alone clearance test.
option_explanations.symptoms_only: Patients can feel well despite residual ventricular or rhythm abnormalities. Symptoms are one domain, not the whole assessment.
option_explanations.cxr_only: Radiography does not directly assess myocardial inflammation or arrhythmia risk and is not the definitive follow-up test.

questions.board_pearl: Recovery from myocarditis is a matrix, not a single number.

evidence.claim: Myocarditis follow-up includes clinical assessment, rhythm evaluation, ventricular imaging, biomarkers, and CMR depending on severity and phenotype.
Pediatric myocarditis follow-up and exercise decisions require assessment beyond symptoms alone.

questions.learning_objective: Interpret persistent LGE as potentially relevant residual injury/scar without overstating pediatric prognostic certainty.
questions.stem: A 14-year-old is asymptomatic after myocarditis and LV systolic function has normalized, but follow-up CMR still shows residual late gadolinium enhancement without clear active edema. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: Residual LGE may represent persistent myocardial injury/scar and can contribute to arrhythmic risk assessment, but its individual prognostic meaning in children should be interpreted with the full clinical picture
Persistent LGE proves ongoing active viral infection
LGE becomes irrelevant once ejection fraction normalizes
Any persistent LGE automatically requires an implanted defibrillator
Rhythm surveillance is unnecessary when EF is normal

questions.rationale: LGE can persist after acute inflammation as residual injury/fibrosis and is associated with arrhythmic risk in broader myocarditis data. Pediatric outcome data are less complete, so LGE should inform—not independently dictate—risk decisions.

option_explanations.lge_relevant: Correct. It preserves the clinically relevant signal while respecting pediatric evidence limitations.
option_explanations.active_infection: LGE is a tissue-injury/scar marker, not a microbiologic test and does not prove ongoing viral replication.
option_explanations.always_benign: Normal EF does not erase scar substrate or automatically make LGE clinically irrelevant.
option_explanations.automatic_icd: Device decisions depend on arrhythmia history, ventricular function, scar extent/location, active inflammation, genetics, and specialist assessment; LGE alone is not a universal pediatric ICD rule.
option_explanations.no_rhythm: Persistent scar may justify continued rhythm assessment depending on the phenotype even when global function is normal.

questions.board_pearl: Persistent LGE can outlast active inflammation; treat it as a risk signal, not a deterministic pediatric prognosis.

evidence.claim: Persistent LGE after myocarditis can represent an arrhythmogenic substrate and contributes to risk stratification.
Pediatric CMR outcome data remain more limited than adult data and should be interpreted cautiously.

questions.learning_objective: Require clinical remission and rhythm/function reassessment before return to strenuous/competitive exercise after myocarditis.
questions.stem: A 16-year-old competitive runner wants to resume full training after myocarditis. Which finding set is most appropriate before considering return to strenuous competition?

options.text: Clinical remission with recovered ventricular function, no important ongoing myocardial injury/inflammation, and no clinically significant arrhythmia on appropriate rhythm/exercise assessment
No chest pain for one week, regardless of cardiac testing
Normal resting ejection fraction regardless of ventricular ectopy or biomarkers
Normal troponin regardless of persistent dysfunction or arrhythmia
Completion of a calendar interval alone, even if recovery testing remains abnormal

questions.rationale: Sports clearance after myocarditis should be based on evidence of clinical recovery across inflammation/injury, ventricular function, and arrhythmia risk. Time restrictions are used in guidance, but a calendar interval alone cannot override persistent abnormalities.

option_explanations.recovery_set: Correct. This captures the central common ground across pediatric AHA and more recent international/ACC frameworks.
option_explanations.symptoms_only: Symptoms can resolve before electrical or tissue recovery. Symptom freedom is necessary but insufficient.
option_explanations.ef_only: Normal EF does not neutralize ventricular arrhythmia or ongoing myocardial injury.
option_explanations.troponin_only: A normal injury marker is reassuring but cannot substitute for function and rhythm reassessment.
option_explanations.time_only: Traditional guidance uses time-based restriction, while newer guidance increasingly individualizes remission. In either model, persistent abnormal testing prevents clearance regardless of elapsed time.

questions.board_pearl: Return to play is a recovery decision, not simply a countdown.

evidence.claim: Pediatric AHA guidance recommends exercise restriction and rhythm/exercise reassessment before return to competitive athletics after myocarditis.
The 2025 ESC guideline emphasizes individualized clinical remission with symptoms, biomarkers, rhythm, and imaging rather than a rigid time definition alone.

questions.learning_objective: Defer sports clearance when clinically significant ventricular arrhythmia persists despite normalized symptoms and EF.
questions.stem: A 15-year-old is asymptomatic months after myocarditis and has normal LV function, but exercise testing produces frequent complex ventricular ectopy. What is the best recommendation?

options.text: Defer competitive sports and continue cardiology/rhythm evaluation
Clear immediately because EF is normal
Clear because the adolescent feels well
Ignore the exercise-induced ectopy if the resting ECG is normal
Increase training intensity to suppress the ectopy through conditioning

questions.rationale: Complex exercise-induced ventricular ectopy indicates persistent electrical risk and is incompatible with routine competitive-sports clearance after myocarditis, even when symptoms and global systolic function have normalized.

option_explanations.defer_sports: Correct. The unresolved recovery domain is rhythm, and it controls the clearance decision until adequately evaluated.
option_explanations.clear_ef: EF does not measure arrhythmia risk; electrical recovery can lag mechanical recovery.
option_explanations.clear_symptoms: Symptom resolution is reassuring but does not neutralize an objectively abnormal exercise rhythm response.
option_explanations.ignore_exercise: Exercise testing is specifically useful because it may reveal arrhythmia not present at rest.
option_explanations.exercise_treatment: Intense exercise is not therapy for potentially pathologic ventricular ectopy after myocarditis and may increase risk.

questions.board_pearl: The last abnormal recovery domain can determine sports clearance—even when everything else looks normal.

evidence.claim: Absence of clinically significant arrhythmia on Holter/exercise assessment is part of return-to-sport evaluation after myocarditis.
Persistent ventricular arrhythmia is an important risk marker in myocarditis follow-up.

questions.learning_objective: Continue longitudinal heart-failure/cardiomyopathy management when ventricular dysfunction persists after the acute myocarditis phase.
questions.stem: A 10-year-old is clinically improved after myocarditis but has persistent mild-to-moderate LV systolic dysfunction at follow-up. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: Persistent dysfunction requires ongoing cardiology/heart-failure follow-up and may represent residual or evolving inflammatory/dilated cardiomyopathy
Persistent dysfunction proves the original myocarditis diagnosis was incorrect
Reduced systolic function is a normal pediatric recovery variant requiring no follow-up
Competitive sports should resume automatically once symptoms resolve
Further imaging is unnecessary because the acute infection has passed

questions.rationale: Myocarditis can resolve completely, leave persistent dysfunction, or evolve into an inflammatory/dilated cardiomyopathy phenotype. Residual LV dysfunction therefore warrants ongoing guideline-directed specialist management and surveillance.

option_explanations.ongoing_cm_follow: Correct. The chronic cardiac phenotype—not the disappearance of the trigger—now drives management.
option_explanations.diagnosis_wrong: Persistent dysfunction is a recognized myocarditis outcome and does not retrospectively disprove the acute inflammatory episode.
option_explanations.normal_variant: Reduced systolic function is pathologic and cannot be dismissed as a normal recovery variant.
option_explanations.sports_auto: Persistent ventricular dysfunction is a reason for continued restriction and individualized reassessment, not automatic clearance.
option_explanations.no_imaging: Serial imaging is needed to document recovery, stability, or progression when ventricular function remains abnormal.

questions.board_pearl: Persistent dysfunction after myocarditis is not the end of the story—it may become a chronic cardiomyopathy problem.

evidence.claim: Pediatric myocarditis outcomes range from complete recovery to persistent dysfunction and chronic heart failure/cardiomyopathy.
Pediatric ADHF requires longitudinal management and discharge/follow-up planning when ventricular dysfunction persists.

questions.learning_objective: Reevaluate persistent exertional symptoms rather than attribute them automatically to deconditioning or anxiety after EF normalizes.
questions.stem: A 14-year-old has normal LV ejection fraction after myocarditis but still develops exertional dyspnea and palpitations. What is the best approach?

options.text: Reassess for residual cardiac dysfunction, arrhythmia, ongoing inflammation/scar, and noncardiac causes before activity clearance
Assume deconditioning without further evaluation because EF is normal
Attribute symptoms to anxiety automatically
Clear for unrestricted sports because EF is normal
Check only troponin and ignore symptoms if it is normal

questions.rationale: Persistent exertional symptoms after myocarditis require explanation. EF may normalize while arrhythmia, subtle dysfunction, tissue injury, deconditioning, pulmonary disease, or other causes persist.

option_explanations.reassess: Correct. The appropriate response is broad reassessment rather than diagnostic closure on one recovered parameter.
option_explanations.deconditioning: Deconditioning is plausible after activity restriction but should be a conclusion after important cardiac causes have been reassessed.
option_explanations.anxiety: Anxiety can coexist with recovery but should not be used to dismiss exertional cardiac symptoms without evaluation.
option_explanations.clear: Normal EF alone is not sufficient when exertional symptoms remain unexplained.
option_explanations.troponin_only: Normal troponin does not exclude arrhythmia or residual scar and cannot substitute for symptom-directed evaluation.

questions.board_pearl: Normal EF narrows the problem; it does not explain persistent symptoms.

evidence.claim: Myocarditis follow-up should integrate symptoms with rhythm, imaging, and other clinical data before exercise clearance.
Pediatric myocarditis recovery assessment includes function and rhythm rather than EF alone.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize that a child who required MCS or had malignant arrhythmia needs longer and more intensive follow-up than an uncomplicated chest-pain phenotype.
questions.stem: A 7-year-old survived fulminant myocarditis requiring VA-ECMO and had ventricular tachycardia during the admission. Ventricular function later normalizes. Which follow-up principle is best?

options.text: Continue longitudinal cardiology follow-up with rhythm and imaging surveillance tailored to the prior complicated phenotype
Discharge permanently from cardiac follow-up because EF normalized
Repeat testing only if the family reports chest pain
Rhythm surveillance is unnecessary once ECMO is discontinued
Full athletic participation is appropriate immediately after EF recovery

questions.rationale: A complicated presentation involving MCS and ventricular arrhythmia carries greater residual risk than an uncomplicated phenotype. Functional recovery is favorable but does not eliminate the need for longer-term rhythm and structural/tissue surveillance.

option_explanations.longitudinal_highrisk: Correct. Initial severity and residual findings should determine the intensity and duration of follow-up.
option_explanations.discharge_forever: Normal EF is encouraging but does not erase the prior malignant electrical/hemodynamic phenotype.
option_explanations.symptoms_only: Asymptomatic arrhythmia or residual scar can occur, so symptom-triggered testing alone is insufficient in a previously complicated case.
option_explanations.no_rhythm: Prior ventricular tachycardia specifically supports continued rhythm surveillance during recovery.
option_explanations.sports_immediate: Sports return requires a structured recovery assessment and is not based on EF normalization alone.

questions.board_pearl: The initial severity phenotype should follow the patient into the follow-up plan.

evidence.claim: Complicated myocarditis requires structured follow-up with clinical, rhythm, and imaging reassessment.
Pediatric fulminant myocarditis survivors can recover ventricular function after ECMO but require ongoing cardiac care.

questions.learning_objective: Select a follow-up battery that measures mechanical, electrical, and tissue recovery rather than repeating only the acute diagnostic marker.
questions.stem: A 13-year-old is several months out from myocarditis with an initially arrhythmic presentation. Which combination best addresses the major residual cardiac risks before higher-intensity activity?

options.text: Clinical assessment plus ECG/rhythm monitoring, ventricular imaging, exercise assessment when appropriate, and CMR/biomarkers guided by the initial phenotype and prior abnormalities
Troponin alone
Chest radiograph alone
Echocardiography alone regardless of prior arrhythmia or CMR abnormalities
Symptom questionnaire alone

questions.rationale: Mechanical function, rhythm, active injury/inflammation, and scar can evolve independently. Follow-up after an arrhythmic myocarditis phenotype should assess those domains rather than repeat a single acute marker.

option_explanations.full_reassessment: Correct. The exact test set is individualized, but this combination covers the principal residual risks.
option_explanations.troponin: Troponin does not assess ventricular function, exercise-provoked arrhythmia, or residual scar.
option_explanations.cxr: Radiography may be useful for pulmonary congestion in selected contexts but is not a comprehensive myocarditis-recovery tool.
option_explanations.echo_only: Echo is essential for function but cannot replace rhythm evaluation or tissue characterization when those were abnormal initially.
option_explanations.symptoms: Symptoms are important but can underestimate silent electrical or imaging abnormalities.

questions.board_pearl: Follow-up testing should mirror the domains that were dangerous during the acute illness.

evidence.claim: Myocarditis follow-up includes clinical assessment, ECG/Holter, exercise testing when appropriate, echocardiography, biomarkers, and CMR according to risk and prior findings.
Pediatric myocarditis return-to-activity assessment includes Holter and exercise testing in athletes.

questions.learning_objective: Avoid answering return-to-sport questions with a calendar interval alone when current guidance requires recovery criteria and recommendations differ by document/population.
questions.stem: A 16-year-old asks, 'Exactly how many months after myocarditis am I automatically safe to compete again?' Which response best reflects guideline-based reasoning?

options.text: No calendar interval by itself guarantees safety; US pediatric guidance has traditionally used a months-long restriction and reassessment, while newer international guidance emphasizes individualized clinical remission, so recovery testing and local pediatric cardiology guidance determine clearance
Every child is automatically safe after exactly one month
Every child is automatically safe at exactly six months even with persistent arrhythmia or dysfunction
Normal EF permits immediate return regardless of time, biomarkers, CMR, or rhythm
Any history of myocarditis permanently prohibits competitive sports

questions.rationale: Traditional US pediatric guidance has used a 3-to-6-month framework with reassessment, whereas newer international guidance increasingly individualizes return based on clinical remission. The common safety principle is that elapsed time cannot override persistent symptoms, injury, dysfunction, inflammation, or arrhythmia.

option_explanations.guideline_context: Correct. This avoids mixing guideline eras and populations while preserving the clinically important recovery criteria.
option_explanations.one_month_all: A universal one-month rule is not supported for pediatric myocarditis and ignores phenotype severity and residual abnormalities.
option_explanations.six_month_all: A months-long interval has been used in prior guidance, but six months does not automatically clear a patient with persistent VT, LV dysfunction, or active inflammation.
option_explanations.ef_immediate: Mechanical recovery alone cannot establish electrical or inflammatory recovery.
option_explanations.never: Many patients ultimately return to activity after appropriate recovery and risk assessment; lifelong prohibition is not universal.

questions.board_pearl: When guidelines evolve, anchor to the shared safety criteria and state which population/document supplies any time interval.

evidence.claim: The AHA pediatric statement summarizes return-to-competition guidance using a 3-to-6-month restriction with rhythm/exercise reassessment.
The 2025 ESC guideline emphasizes individualized return after clinical remission rather than relying exclusively on fixed time definitions.

questions.learning_objective: Integrate hemodynamic, electrical, functional, and follow-up readiness before discharge rather than use symptom improvement alone.
questions.stem: An 11-year-old was admitted with myocarditis, moderate LV dysfunction, and nonsustained VT. Symptoms have improved and the child is asking to go home. Which discharge principle is safest?

options.text: Discharge should follow demonstrated clinical/hemodynamic stability, an acceptable rhythm plan, a defined ventricular-function trajectory, medication/family education as applicable, and arranged cardiology follow-up with activity restrictions
Discharge as soon as chest pain resolves regardless of rhythm or ventricular function
Discharge once troponin begins to fall even if ventricular tachycardia recurs
Discharge if oxygen saturation is normal despite persistent poor perfusion
No cardiology follow-up is needed if the child can walk normally at discharge

questions.rationale: Safe discharge after myocarditis—especially an arrhythmic, ventricular-dysfunction presentation—requires more than symptom improvement. The child needs stable physiology, a clear rhythm and ventricular assessment, education, restrictions, and a longitudinal follow-up plan.

option_explanations.discharge_integrated: Correct. It translates the multidomain nature of myocarditis into a practical disposition decision.
option_explanations.symptoms_enough: Chest symptoms can resolve while ventricular dysfunction or arrhythmia persists; symptom relief alone is insufficient.
option_explanations.troponin_enough: A falling biomarker does not neutralize recurrent VT or persistent pump failure.
option_explanations.spo2_enough: Pulse oximetry does not measure systemic cardiac output or electrical stability.
option_explanations.no_followup: Functional appearance at discharge does not eliminate recurrence, residual dysfunction, or sports/activity considerations.

questions.board_pearl: Discharge myocarditis only when the physiology, rhythm, function, education, and follow-up plan are all ready—not when one symptom improves.

evidence.claim: Pediatric acute decompensated heart failure discharge planning requires clinical stability, education, and structured follow-up.
Myocarditis follow-up requires longitudinal assessment of function, rhythm, and activity readiness.
